exercises.approach: Convert p with ggplotly, build it, and keep only scatter traces whose mode contains markers before collecting x and y.
exercises.why: Mapping colour to group splits the four points into two marker traces, A with (1, 1) and (2, 3) and B with (3, 2) and (4, 6). The observations are the points inside those traces, not the traces themselves.
exercises.wrong: Counting the entries of the built data list as observations. This plot yields 2, one per colour, and a plot with a reference line yields more, so the count tracks legend entries rather than rows of d.

exercises.approach: Join each marker's x and y into one key with paste(x, y, sep = ":") and compare the sorted keys with the same keys built from d.
exercises.why: d holds the pairs 1:1, 2:3, 3:2 and 4:6. A key keeps each response attached to its input, so a translation that shuffled responses between inputs would no longer match.
exercises.wrong: Comparing sort(xs) with sort(d$x) and sort(ys) with sort(d$y) separately. If the first two responses were swapped, giving pairs 1:3 and 2:1, both sorted vectors would still be 1, 2, 3, 4 and 1, 2, 3, 6, so the check would pass.

exercises.approach: Add geom_hline at mean(d$y), convert it again, and count markers only in traces whose mode contains markers.
exercises.why: The responses sum to 12, so the dashed line sits at 3. ggplotly draws it as an extra line trace across the panel, which adds geometry and x values but no observations.
exercises.wrong: Summing the length of x over every trace. The line trace contributes its own x values, so the total exceeds 4 and the reference line is counted as data.

exercises.approach: Pass tooltip = c("x", "y", "group") so the hover shows only the input, the response and the group for each point.
exercises.why: Those three fields identify a point in this fixture. The tooltip labels come from the variable names x, y and group rather than the axis titles Input and Response, so readable wording must be supplied deliberately, for example through a text aesthetic.
exercises.wrong: Leaving the default of all mapped aesthetics. In a richer plot that also exposes fields such as size or alpha, which mean nothing to a reader, and it still does not show the axis titles.
exercises.verify: `grepl("group: A", traces[[1]]$text[1], fixed = TRUE)` returns TRUE, and a browser hover shows whether that wording is readable.

exercises.approach: List the properties the conversion call does not establish and check them on the two printed figures side by side.
exercises.why: The payload checks confirm four points with the right pairs. They say nothing about legend order, whether size 3 becomes a comparable marker size, whether the Group legend title and axis titles carry over, or how the widget fits its container.
exercises.wrong: Stating that the interactive figure matches the static one because ggplotly returned without error. Conversion can succeed while dropping or restyling parts of the ggplot specification.
exercises.verify: Viewing print(p) and print(interactive) together in a browser shows any difference in legend order, marker size or titles.

exercises.approach: Build the figure directly with plot_ly when the interaction needs IDs, named traces or buttons with known positions.
exercises.why: This fixture has no ID column, and ggplotly decides how many traces to create and in which order. A direct specification fixes both, so customdata and visibility vectors can be checked against an intended layout.
exercises.wrong: Patching the converted widget by index, such as editing the third entry of its data list. The index depends on how the translator split the layers, so the edit can land on the wrong trace after a change to the ggplot.
exercises.verify: A direct plot_ly version with two add_trace calls returns exactly 2 traces from plotly_build.
